Measures Across Studies
This page lists the full materials for each study: the Pilot Study 1 narrative codebook and, for Pilot Study 2, Study 1 and Study 2, the vignette page participants read in each condition, with the document images that page shows, in order. Each vignette page is the participant-facing page embedded in the survey; it also holds the instructions and the text passages participants read between the images. The images here are reduced copies; the vignette pages show them at full size.
Selected stimulus images, full materials, and item wording are linked in the Pilot Study 2 materials, Study 1 materials, and Study 2 materials. The shared individual-difference scales and demographic items are in the dissertation’s Individual-Difference Scales and Demographic Items section.
Table 2 lists the measures administered in each study and the changes in wording, response scale, or compositing rules between studies. All three studies shared a core of scenario-dependent judgment measures and individual-difference scales; Study 2 added several measures that the earlier studies did not include.

title: Study Materials
text: Note. Yes = administered; — = not administered. Three structural differences run through the table. First, Pilot 2 and Study 1 used a search-warrant paradigm, in which the detective sought a warrant and participants evaluated the search, whereas Study 2 used an arrest paradigm, in which the detective arrested the suspect and participants served as jurors evaluating probable cause and damages; the referent wording changed accordingly. Second, Pilot 2 and Study 1 referred to “the suspect,” whereas Study 2 named the suspect (Ms. Johnston) and the detective (Detective Snyder). Third, Study 1 tensed its items by cell (present or future tense in foresight, past tense in hindsight), whereas Study 2 used the past tense throughout, with a conditional framing (“as if you did not know”) in the no-outcome condition. Individual-difference scale items and attention checks were identical across the three studies.

title: Pilot Study 1
text:
About this document
This part includes the supplementary analyses for Pilot Study 1. The Pilot Study 1 materials include the registered models and hypotheses, narrative-coding reliability checks, and exploratory analyses supporting Chapter 5.

title: Pilot Study 1 Design and Materials
text:
Card-Sorting Task Materials
Pilot Study 1 combined narrative writing, card sorting, and individual-difference measures. I assigned each participant to one of four verdict conditions for the narrative task; within that condition, participants wrote about all four crime prompts. They then evaluated the same set of 20 cards and completed the attitude measures and demographics. Table P1.1 links the tasks and coding materials, and Figure P1.1 separates the participant sequence from narrative coding after collection.
The registered task description gives the full instructions and all 20 cards; the registered measures give the questions and response options. The narrative coding workbook contains the codebook and coding instructions. These files are also linked from the study materials hub.
The card-sorting task is described in the Pilot 1 Method in Chapter 5 of the dissertation. In brief, I presented 20 short pregnancy-related experiences in random order, adapting the card-sort method of VandeVusse et al. (2023). Participants answered three questions about each card, each with three response options: whether the scenario could describe a crime, whether it is a crime where they live, and whether it should be. The three questions are my own. After sorting all 20 cards, participants picked the five they had found hardest to sort and wrote a brief explanation for each.
Table P1.2 lists the 20 card stems with the six features I coded for each: the mental-state cue, medical intervention, gestational age, method, care-seeking, and pregnancy outcome.

title: Registered Analytic Models and Hypotheses
text:
Analytic Models.
I conducted all analyses in R (R Core Team, 2026). Each research question was tested with its own model. Chi-square tests of independence compared the content of the narratives across the four crime categories (RQ1) and across the four verdict conditions (RQ2). These tests covered the 67 automated features (i.e., the Phase 1 and Phase 2 codes), with the Benjamini–Hochberg correction applied across that family. The 14 holistic codes (i.e., the Phase 3 codes) are complete. However, only one provided interpretable evidence that the preregistered reliability target had been met. I therefore used the holistic codes only in the analyses of mitigating and aggravating factors and mental states (H2a, H2b, H2c, and H3a), and I treat every result that rests on a holistic code as exploratory. I report Cramér’s V with a 95% confidence interval for each variable.
A within-subjects one-way ANOVA tested whether post-narrative severity ratings differed across the four crime categories (RQ3, H3b). Each participant gave four ratings, one for each crime category. I applied the Greenhouse–Geisser correction when sphericity was violated. I fit the ANOVA with the afex package, computed estimated marginal means and planned contrasts with emmeans (Lenth & Piaskowski, 2017), and computed effect sizes with the effectsize package. Registered planned contrasts and main effects were tested at α = .05 without adjustment. The one exception was the follow-up of interactions. I corrected the simple effects that probe the interaction of verdict condition and factor type (H2b) within that family. I used Tukey’s HSD when the follow-up compared all pairs of estimated marginal means and the Bonferroni correction when it tested a specified subset.
Two multiple regressions tested whether scores on the Modified Abortion Attitudes Scale predicted each participant’s mean severity and mean punishment ratings across the four crime categories (RQ4, H4). Age, political orientation, and religiosity were covariates. I compared the card-sort consensus with the preregistered threshold descriptively (RQ5). Mixed-effects logistic regressions tested whether the features of each scenario predicted the binary judgment that the scenario was “definitely yes, this is a crime” (H5). Each model had a random intercept for participants. I fit these models with the lme4 and lmerTest packages. A pooled McNemar’s test across the 20 scenarios compared descriptive and normative crime judgments (RQ6, H6). The legal-accuracy analysis used one-sample binomial tests against chance (.50), for each scenario and pooled across scenarios. I computed the McNemar and exact binomial tests with the exact2x2 package. Two mixed-effects logistic regressions of the card-sort crime judgments tested the attitude hypotheses (RQ7, H7a and H7b). The first model pooled the two judgment types. The second added the interaction of abortion attitudes and judgment type. Both models had crossed random intercepts for participants and scenarios, and both were fit with lme4 and lmerTest.
I report effect sizes (i.e., partial \(\eta^2\), Cramér’s V, and odds ratios) and 95% confidence intervals for all tests. The cluster analysis is exploratory. It used partitioning around medoids on Gower distance within each crime category. I fit it with the cluster package and evaluated it with the silhouette width and the gap statistic. I computed scale descriptives and reliability coefficients with the psych package. The text analyses of the narratives used quanteda (Benoit et al., 2018), with quanteda.textstats and quanteda.textplots for keyness and text statistics and udpipe for linguistic annotation. I computed inter-rater reliability (i.e., Cohen’s and Fleiss’s kappa) with the irr package.
The two kinds of mixed-effects logistic regression take the following multilevel form. In the feature-prediction models (H5), crime judgments \(i\) are nested within participants \(j\). Each scenario feature \(F\) enters as a single Level-1 predictor:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Level 1:} \quad & \mathrm{logit}\big(\mathrm{Pr}(\text{crime}_{ij} = 1)\big) = \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1}\,F_{ij} \\
\text{Level 2:} \quad & \beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j}, \quad u_{0j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \tau^{2}_{\text{participant}}).
\end{aligned}
\]
The attitude models (H7a and H7b) cross each judgment with both participants \(j\) and scenarios \(k\). Standardized abortion attitudes (\(\text{AAS}_j\)) enter as a participant-level (Level-2) predictor, and judgment type (descriptive vs. normative) enters as a Level-1 predictor:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Level 1:} \quad & \mathrm{logit}\big(\mathrm{Pr}(\text{crime}_{ijk} = 1)\big) = \beta_{0jk} + \beta_{1jk}\,\text{JudgmentType}_{ijk} \\
\text{Level 2:} \quad & \beta_{0jk} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01}\,\text{AAS}_{j} + u_{0j} + v_{0k} \\
& \beta_{1jk} = \gamma_{10} + \gamma_{11}\,\text{AAS}_{j} \\
& u_{0j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \tau^{2}_{\text{participant}}), \quad v_{0k} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \tau^{2}_{\text{scenario}}).
\end{aligned}
\]
H7b tests whether the association between abortion attitudes and crime judgments differs by judgment type (\(\gamma_{11}\)). H7a tests the main-effects model, in which \(\gamma_{11} = 0\).

text:
Narrative Features by Verdict Condition (RQ2)
This chapter reports the analyses of the narratives by verdict condition (RQ2, H2a, H2b, and H2c) and three exploratory analyses. These are the accuracy of participants’ legal judgments, the three-way interaction of abortion attitudes, state law, and judgment type, and the comparison of the narratives with television plotlines and documented cases.
A series of descriptive chi-square tests compared the frequency of each feature across the four verdict conditions, with the Benjamini–Hochberg correction applied across the testable features (RQ2; see Table P1.16). After correction, the four verdict conditions differed on 12 narrative features. These included legal terminology, \(\chi^2(3, N = 311) = 28.98\), BH-adjusted p < .001. For causal structure, the association with verdict condition was Cramér’s V = .29.

title: Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy
section: Coded Factors by Verdict Condition (H2a and H2b)
text:
Coded Factors by Verdict Condition (H2a and H2b)
H2a predicted that narratives written toward a wrongful verdict would contain more coded mitigating and aggravating factors than narratives written toward a rightful verdict. There was no significant difference in total coded factors per narrative across the four verdict conditions, F(3, 76) = 0.88, MSe = 0.33, p = .456, \(\eta^2\) = .034. Contrary to H2a, narratives in the wrongful conditions (M = 1.00, SD = 0.56) did not contain significantly more coded factors than narratives in the rightful conditions (M = 0.80, SD = 0.57; see Figure P1.3).



Figure P1.3
Pilot 1 Coded Factors by Verdict Condition












Note. Estimated marginal mean of total coded factors per narrative by verdict condition, from the H2a one-way ANOVA. Error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals.




H2b predicted that the wrongful–rightful difference would be larger for mitigating than for aggravating factors. There was no significant interaction between verdict condition and factor type, F(3, 76) = 0.59, MSe = 0.13, p = .622, \(\eta_p^2\) = .023. Contrary to H2b, the wrongful–rightful difference was not larger for mitigating factors. However, there was a significant main effect of factor type: narratives contained more mitigating factors (M = 0.50, SD = 0.37) than aggravating factors (M = 0.39, SD = 0.39; F(1, 76) = 4.54, MSe = 0.13, p = .036, \(\eta_p^2\) = .056).
crumbs: 6  Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy

title: Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy
text:
Mental State by Actual Culpability (H2c)
H2c rests on the coded mental-state category, so I report it as exploratory. H2c predicted that narratives in the culpable conditions would attribute purposeful or knowing mental states more often than narratives in the non-culpable conditions. The relationship between actual culpability and coded mental state was not significant, \(\chi^2\)(1, N = 279) = 0.32, p = .572. Contrary to H2c, coded mental state did not differ by actual culpability. However, the mental-state code did not meet the preregistered reliability target (ICC = .67, registered \(\kappa\) = .43, target = .80; see Table P1.5), leaving this result inconclusive. The code was not reliable enough to tell whether participants matched the mental state to the verdict they wrote toward or to the facts of the case.

title: Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy
section: Legal Accuracy of the Crime Judgments
text:
Legal Accuracy of the Crime Judgments
State-law coding. For the legal-accuracy sub-analysis, participants’ descriptive judgments (“Is this a crime where you live?”) were compared with the legal status of each scenario in their state of residence as of May 2026. Participant responses were matched based on accuracy (yes/no). However, given that the specifics of state laws regarding abortion remain in flux and convoluted, I did not interpret a mismatch as true ignorance of the underlying state-specific status. For example, many state abortion bans do not apply to pregnant people as a matter of black letter law, but they still can be, and have been, used to criminalize abortion (Weigel et al., 2020), so whether self-managed abortion is a crime in a given state is not a clear binary. The coding rules, sources, and confidence flags used in the preregistered sensitivity analysis appear in State-Law Coding for the Legal-Accuracy Sub-Analysis and Table P1.17.

State-Law Coding for the Legal-Accuracy Sub-Analysis
The legal-accuracy sub-analysis compared each participant’s answer to the descriptive question (“Is this a crime where you live?”) with the current legal status of each of the 20 scenarios in the participant’s reported state. To do this I drew on several existing sources. These were the Center for Reproductive Rights’ “After Roe Fell” map as of May 2026 (Center for Reproductive Rights, 2026), Pregnancy Justice’s After Pregnancy Loss report (Pregnancy Justice, 2026), the NCSL’s fetal-homicide compilation (National Conference of State Legislatures, 2018), and the appellate case law in Aspinwall (2023), Bach & Wasilczuk (2025), and Darlington et al. (2021). Table P1.17 provides the basic coding scheme.

A few scenarios called for a judgment. The legal status of the inchoate-conduct scenarios is unclear, so I assigned them low confidence. The miscarriage-management scenarios and home disposal after a miscarriage are not defined as crimes in their own right. I therefore coded them under the general abuse-of-corpse or concealment statutes (Pregnancy Justice, 2026; Rinkunas, 2026). I assigned medium confidence to the substance-use scenario on the basis of appellate decisions in Alabama, South Carolina, and Oklahoma (Aspinwall, 2023). Most cases with known pregnancy outcomes in the documented sample involved live births, however, limiting their relevance to the fetal-death scenario (Bach & Wasilczuk, 2025). Confidence was also medium for the accident scenario and low for the omission-of-care scenarios. Most fetal-homicide statutes exempt the pregnant woman (National Conference of State Legislatures, 2018; Unborn Victims of Violence Act of 2004, 2004), and no statute makes delaying or failing to report care a crime on its own (Pregnancy Justice, 2026).
I report the legal-accuracy analysis as exploratory. Compared with the state-law coding, accuracy differed significantly from chance on 19 of the 20 scenarios. Accuracy on the 13 state-invariant scenarios ranged from .70 to 1.00 (M = .96) and was lower on average on the six abortion scenarios with between-state variance (.64 to .82, M = .76). The per-scenario accuracy tallies appear in Table P1.15.

title: Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy
section: Abortion Attitudes, State Law, and Judgment Type
text:
Abortion Attitudes, State Law, and Judgment Type
I report this analysis as exploratory. When the state-law coding was added to the mixed-effects model of card-sort crime judgments, the three-way Attitudes × State Law × Judgment Type interaction was significant (OR = 0.28, 95% CI [0.13, 0.63], z = −3.09, p = .002; see Table P1.13). The pilot was not powered for the three-way interaction, so I report that estimate descriptively.

section: Comparisons With Television and Documented Cases
text:
Comparisons With Television and Documented Cases
Table P1.18 compares the methods specified in the narratives with the procedures visually depicted in U.S. television plotlines (Herold & Sisson, 2019). The automated Section J code found no references to actual cases in the 311 narratives.
I used Pregnancy Justice (2023); the registered television source provided no comparable prosecution figures. For chemical endangerment, I used the criminal child neglect, abuse, or endangerment category (.84 of cases with known charges). I used .06 for fetal homicide and .01 for self-managed abortion. For improper disposal, I added two Pregnancy Justice categories together: tampering with remains or abuse of a corpse (.02) and failure to report a birth or death (.01), for .03. One case could carry charges in more than one category, however, so the categories can overlap.
The prompts, in contrast, were split evenly across the four crimes, at about .25 each. Compared with the prosecutions, then, the prompts gave more weight to fetal homicide, self-managed abortion, and improper disposal and less to chemical endangerment. Because the design fixed those shares, the narrative proportions cannot show how common participants believe each crime to be.

About this document
This part includes the full analyses for Pilot Study 2. Chapter 5 of the dissertation reports the hypotheses and main results. Here I report the analytic framework and hypotheses, the full results with their tables and figures, and the supplementary, exploratory, and robustness analyses.

0% — 100% per outcome · Four items, fixed order, rated independently; ratings need not sum to 100%.
Pre-search instructions (foresight framing): “You are the judge who has been asked to authorize this search. The search reveals evidence that the suspect illegally obtained an abortion to end her own pregnancy. ____%

section: G. Ratings of the Search Scenario
text:
G. Ratings of the Search Scenario
Two 9-point subscales (believability; relevance) · 10 narrative evidence items, the same list at every administration · Each subscale is administered as a 10-statement matrix with drop-down responses, the instruction as the matrix stem on the same page, and statement order randomized per participant.
The relevance dimension is adapted from the Casper et al. (1989) and Robbennolt & Sobus (1997) evidence-reinterpretation paradigm. The believability dimension is taken verbatim from Marshall (2022).

G.a Believability Ratings
Instructions (matrix stem, pre-search only): “Please rate how believable you think it is that each of the following items from the situation leading up to the search would actually occur in a real life situation:”
Response: 9-point scale (1 = not at all believable to 9 = extremely believable), one rating per evidence item.


G.b Relevance Ratings (Casper et al., 1989)
Pre-search instructions (future tense, foresight variant; matrix stem): “Next, we would like you to rate how relevant you think each of the following items from the situation leading up to the search would be to what would actually be found as a result of the search of the suspect’s phone:”
Post-search instructions (past tense, hindsight variant; matrix stem): “Next, we would like you to rate how relevant you think each of the following items from the situation leading up to the search were to what was actually found as a result of the search of the suspect’s phone:”
Response: 9-point scale (1 = not at all relevant to 9 = extremely relevant), one rating per evidence item.

text:
I. Suspect’s Moral Culpability (Post-Search Only) (Alicke, 2000)
Three single-item 7-point measures, rated separately (no composite); anchors as shown per item.
Blame item (1 = not at all blameworthy to 7 = extremely blameworthy): “To what extent is the suspect blameworthy for what happened?”
Responsibility item (1 = not at all responsible to 7 = completely responsible): “How responsible is the suspect for what happened?”
Punishment item (1 = no punishment at all to 7 = very severe punishment): “How much punishment does the suspect deserve for what happened?”

Multi-Model Blame Items (Alicke et al., 2008; Cushman et al., 2008; Malle et al., 2014)
Five single-item 7-point measures, rated separately; anchors as shown per item.
Causality item (1 = not at all a cause to 7 = very strong cause): “To what extent did the suspect’s actions cause the pregnancy loss?” Verbatim from Alicke et al. (2008) (Study 1), anchor adapted from 11-point to 7-point.
Reasons item (1 = not at all justified to 7 = completely justified): “Did the suspect have justified reasons for her conduct during the pregnancy?” We wrote this item, grounded in the Guglielmo & Malle (2017) Table 1 reasons template.
Preventability item (1 = definitely not to 7 = definitely yes): “Could the suspect have prevented the pregnancy loss?” Single combined unintentional-branch item. We wrote this item, grounded in the Guglielmo & Malle (2017) Table 1 preventability template.
Character item (1 = very unfavorable to 7 = very favorable): “Given what you know about the suspect from these case materials, do you have a generally favorable or unfavorable impression of her?” Verbatim from Alicke et al. (2008) (Study 3), anchor adapted from 11-point to 7-point.
Wrongness item (1 = not at all to 4 = somewhat to 7 = very much): “Was the suspect’s conduct during the pregnancy morally wrong?” Verbatim from Cushman et al. (2008) (Experiment 1).

text:
K. Search-Target Endorsement (Pre-Search, Administered Once)
Target 1: Reverse keyword warrant (lowest invasiveness). “A court order directing a technology company to identify any person who recently searched for specified pregnancy-related or abortion-related terms on the company’s search engine.” (Kerr, 2025)
Target 2: Provider text-message content warrant (moderate invasiveness). “A warrant served on the suspect’s cellular-service provider compelling disclosure of the content of the suspect’s text messages.” (Stored Communications Act § 2703(d)) (Conti-Cook & Bertash, 2021; Dellinger & Pell, 2024)
Target 3: Physical home search (highest invasiveness). “A warrant authorizing law enforcement officers to physically search the suspect’s home.” (Baucum et al., 2018)

Binary endorsement. “Would you approve of a law enforcement officer conducting this search?” (Yes / No)
Certainty threshold. “What percentage certain would you have to be that the suspect committed the offense described in the affidavit before approving this search?” (0–100 slider, labeled Certainty required (0–100%))
Probability of evidence given guilt. “If the suspect had indeed committed the offense described in the affidavit, what is the probability that this search would uncover evidence of it?” (0–100 slider, labeled Probability (0–100%)) (Baucum et al., 2018).

L. Manipulation Checks

L.a Per-Scenario Comprehension Check
Prompt (in every vignette block): “Please indicate which of the following statements are true about the case you just read. Check all that apply.”
SMA vignette (Mary Hansen)

The suspect identified in the affidavit was named Mary Hansen.
The suspect told the detective she had visited a single telemedicine appointment with an unnamed provider.
The suspect called emergency services immediately after the pregnancy loss.

NCM vignette (Mary Johnston)

The suspect identified in the affidavit was named Mary Johnston.
The suspect was married and had been actively trying to conceive.
The suspect did not disclose the pregnancy to her workplace.

CM vignette (Mary Larson)

The suspect identified in the affidavit was named Mary Larson.
The suspect tried to flush the remains but the toilet backed up, then placed the remains in a bag and put it in the trash.
The suspect disclosed the pregnancy to her boyfriend.

In every block, items 1 and 2 are true and item 3 is false; the three were presented in random order.


L.b Manipulation Check
Item: “What did the search reveal at the end of each affidavit you read?”

Evidence consistent with the suspect’s intentional termination of the pregnancy, concealment of the loss, or improper disposal of remains (correct in the HACE condition)
Evidence of unrelated credit-card fraud (correct in the HUCE condition)
I cannot recall what the search revealed

Options were presented in random order. A participant passed the check by selecting the option that matched their assigned outcome.

title: Analytic Framework and Hypotheses
text:
Analytic Framework.
I conducted the analyses in R (R Core Team, 2026), using Bayesian multilevel models in brms (Bürkner, 2017, 2018) to account for the repeated ratings within participants. Non-criminal miscarriage was the reference scenario. I computed planned contrasts with marginaleffects (Arel-Bundock et al., 2024) and summarized indirect effects from the posterior draws (Falk et al., 2023; Makowski et al., 2019; Miočević et al., 2018; Vuorre & Bolger, 2018). I assessed the effects using their 95% credible intervals (Kruschke & Liddell, 2018).
The preregistration allowed frequentist mixed factorial ANOVAs of the continuous outcomes. The analysis plan also included a GEE check of search-target endorsement. I evaluated the registered hypotheses with the Bayesian decision rules. This supplement reports the Bayesian results.
The multilevel models take the following form. \(Y\) is a continuous outcome measured on occasion \(t\) (i.e., before or after the outcome, or the vignette) within participant \(j\). The kind of incriminating evidence found, \(\text{Outcome}_j\), varies between participants:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Level 1:} \quad & Y_{tj} = \pi_{0j} + \pi_{1j}\,W_{tj} + e_{tj}, \quad e_{tj} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \sigma^{2}) \\
\text{Level 2:} \quad & \pi_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01}\,\text{Outcome}_{j} + u_{0j} \\
& \pi_{1j} = \gamma_{10} + \gamma_{11}\,\text{Outcome}_{j} + u_{1j} \\
& (u_{0j},\ u_{1j})^{\top} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\ \mathbf{T}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(W_{tj}\) is the within-participant factor (i.e., before or after the outcome, or the vignette). The within-participant change is represented by \(\gamma_{10}\), with \(\gamma_{11}\) representing how that change depends on the kind of evidence found. Participant intercepts and slopes have covariance matrix \(\mathbf{T}\). For binary search-target endorsement, I retained the Level-2 structure and modeled \(\mathrm{logit}\big(\mathrm{Pr}(Y_{tj} = 1)\big)\) in place of \(Y_{tj}\), without a Level-1 residual term.
I used mean-zero Normal priors for the regression coefficients, with widths matched to the outcome scales to provide weak regularization. The log-odds coefficients of the binary-choice models had a similarly weak prior (Bürkner, 2018; Gelman et al., 2008; Gelman et al., 2014; Hox et al., 2018; Sorensen et al., 2016). I used an LKJ(2) prior for correlations among participant random effects and retained the scale-aware Student-t defaults in brms for intercepts, random-effect standard deviations, and residual standard deviations (Bürkner, 2017, 2018). For the H5a sensitivity check, I refit the model with half and twice the coefficient-prior widths (Depaoli et al., 2020; Hox et al., 2018). Table P2.4 gives the prior for each parameter class.

I fit the brms models with four chains per data set (Bürkner, 2017, 2018). The default chain length was 4,000 iterations, including 1,000 warmup, with longer chains when needed for convergence. The primary H5a and matched-item models used five completed data sets and 32,000 iterations per chain, including 8,000 warmup. I required R̂ < 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes > 400, and no divergent transitions (Vehtari et al., 2021).

title: Registered Analyses Reported in the Supplement
text:
Content Match: Subjective Probability of Guilt (H2a)
Of the three registered predictions reported here, H2a concerned whether guilt-probability ratings changed more after expected than unexpected evidence, particularly in the two criminal-conduct scenarios. I expected the narrative-prototype ordering of the scenarios to hold for pregnancy-specific likelihood changes after expected evidence (H2c), and the Model Penal Code culpability hierarchy to hold for mental-state ratings within each evidence condition (H5d). None of the three predictions met all registered support criteria.
For the observed means and standard deviations, I averaged each participant’s ratings over the three scenarios. Model estimates are posterior medians with 95% HDIs; probability of direction (pd) is the proportion of draws with the median’s sign. Differences in likelihood and guilt probability retain the 0–100 units.
I predicted that, after expected incriminating evidence, participants would inflate the subjective probability of the suspect’s guilt relative to their own pre-search ratings, more so than after unexpected incriminating evidence, and more so in the self-managed abortion and criminal miscarriage scenarios than in the non-criminal miscarriage scenario (H2a).
Consistent with the first part of H2a, the change in the subjective probability of the suspect’s guilt from before to after the search outcome was larger after expected than after unexpected incriminating evidence (the RH2.1 row of Table P2.7). After expected incriminating evidence, ratings rose from before the search outcome (M = 61.16, SD = 22.26) to after it (M = 69.83, SD = 22.81), an estimated change of 8.55, 95% HDI [5.70, 11.36]; after unexpected incriminating evidence, they fell (before: M = 62.55, SD = 24.10; after: M = 54.50, SD = 25.52), an estimated change of −7.94, 95% HDI [−10.73, −5.20]. Contrary to the second part of H2a, the increase after expected incriminating evidence was not reliably larger in the self-managed abortion and criminal miscarriage scenarios than in the non-criminal miscarriage scenario (posterior probability .103, below the registered threshold). Descriptively, it was largest in the non-criminal miscarriage scenario (10.90) and smaller in the self-managed abortion (8.60) and criminal miscarriage (6.16) scenarios.
Registered verdict. Not supported by all registered criteria.

title: Registered Analyses Reported in the Supplement
text:
Inevitability (H2c)
I further predicted that the change in the pregnancy-specific likelihood would follow the narrative-prototype pattern (criminal miscarriage > self-managed abortion > non-criminal miscarriage; H2c).
H2c predicted the largest increase in disposal or concealment likelihood in the criminal miscarriage scenario after expected incriminating evidence. However, its change did not credibly exceed zero (−0.81, 95% HDI [−5.75, 3.92], pd = 62.9%), nor did the changes in the other two scenarios, and the probability of the predicted ordering was below .001. The non-criminal miscarriage comparison also ran contrary to the prediction: the mean of the two pregnancy items increased (95% HDI [8.43, 15.16]).
Registered verdict. Not supported by all registered criteria. I checked convergence for all parameters and for the registered coefficients separately, using the criteria in Analytic Framework and Hypotheses. The all-parameter check failed. Neither diagnostic reading supported H2c; a failed convergence criterion precludes registered support.

title: Registered Analyses Reported in the Supplement
text:
Mens Rea Hierarchy (H5d)
I predicted the Model Penal Code culpability ordering in participants’ mental-state ratings within each evidence condition (H5d).
H5d was not supported in either evidence condition. Of the adjacent-level contrasts the registered named-step rule requires (purposely minus knowingly and recklessly minus negligently, after each kind of evidence), only purposely minus knowingly after expected incriminating evidence had a 95% HDI above zero; Table P2.28 gives all six contrasts.
Registered verdict. Not supported by all registered criteria.

title: Evidence Reinterpretation (RQ3)
text:
RH1.4 was supported on the respecified item-level model (Table P2.25). The interaction of timing, outcome, and key consistency was 0.77, 95% HDI [0.52, 1.02], Pr(effect > 0) > .999, BF₁₀ > 1000. The 95% HDI meets the registered rule that it lie above zero. The model met the registered convergence criteria.
I respecified the model because the registered model nests item consistency within outcome. The respecified model codes each item, for every participant, by whether it would be consistent with the expected outcome. After inspecting the raw means, I chose to compare the same items across the randomly assigned outcomes. I made that choice before fitting the revised model. That timing makes the test less severe (see item 9.1 of the Pilot 2 deviations record, included in this supplement, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23424192).
The registered model tests the interaction of timing and item consistency, with NCM as the reference vignette (the registered row of Table P2.25). Its 95% HDI meets the registered criterion of a positive interval. Its registered convergence criteria were met (worst within-imputation R-hat = 1.002, lowest effective sample size = 2250, total divergent transitions = 0). In the eight-item sensitivity analysis without items 3 and 10 (added analysis, not registered), the result of the registered model holds (0.68 [0.49, 0.87]). The result of the respecified model does not hold (0.23 [−0.08, 0.54]). Without those two items, its key contrast rests on the NCM vignette alone. The change in the observed composite is descriptive. The exploratory tests for each item below keep the registered grouping by vignette.
The registered model had a divergent transition. To address it, I refit the model on the fourth imputed data set with adapt_delta = .99 (previously .95; added analysis, not registered) and kept the other four fits. The model, priors, data, random seeds, initial values, and iteration counts did not change.

title: Study 1
text:
About this document
The full Study 1 models appear in S4, with additional analyses by research question in S5 through S10. Chapter 5 reports the main findings.
Table and figure numbers identify the study and the section (e.g., Table 1-S4.1 is the first table in S4). I place a table that belongs to several sections in the first one that lists it and use square brackets for references to tables or figures outside this supplement.

title: Study 1 Design and Materials
text:
Condition Materials
In Study 1, I examined judgments of a search warrant after a pregnancy loss using one affidavit carried forward from Pilot Study 2. I randomly assigned each participant to one of six conditions that crossed search-outcome information with the alleged offense. Table S1D.1 links the design to the study materials, and Figure S1D.1 shows the six conditions.
The Materials and Measures chapter reproduces the stimulus variations, survey questions, and response scales. It includes the registered probability-of-guilt item that participants did not see or answer; the deviations record documents that omission. The materials hub provides document-image previews. The preregistration and registered materials PDF provide the planned design and wording.

title: Study 1 Materials and Measures

§ 47-101 — Unauthorized Termination of a Pregnancy; Criminal Abortion. A person commits the offense of unauthorized termination of a pregnancy when he or she (1) knowingly performs, induces, or self-induces an abortion, otherwise than as authorized by law. The offense is punishable as a Class III felony.



§ 47-202 — Improper Disposal of Human Skeletal Remains; Abuse of Corpse. A person commits the offense of improper disposal of human skeletal remains when he or she (1) knowingly removes, abandons, conceals, or otherwise disposes of human skeletal remains. The offense is punishable as a Class III felony.

B. Probable-Cause Judgments
Foresight instructions: “Probable cause exists if all the facts and circumstances, viewed through the lens of common sense, would make a reasonably prudent person think that a search would reveal contraband or evidence of the alleged crime. Based on the description of the facts you just read, is there probable cause to justify the search?”

Based on the description of the facts you just read, was there probable cause to justify the search?”

Probable-cause ruling. (Rachlinski et al., 2011) (Binary; No, there [IS/WAS] not probable cause to justify the search / Yes, there [IS/WAS] probable cause to justify the search)
Confidence in PC ruling. “How confident are you in this decision?” (0–100 slider; 0 = not at all confident, 100 = completely confident)
Subjective probability of guilt. C. Outcome Likelihood Estimates (Fischhoff, 1975; Nestler & Egloff, 2009)
Foresight instructions: “You are the judge who has been asked to authorize this search. Based only on the affidavit you just read and what the detective knew when seeking the warrant, please rate the likelihood of each of the following outcomes of the requested search. There are many possible outcomes; please rate each outcome independently. (0 = not at all likely; 100 = completely likely)”
Hindsight instructions: “Think back to the time when the detective asked you to authorize the search, before it was carried out. Putting yourself back at that moment and deciding based only on what was known then, as if you did not know what the search ultimately revealed, please rate the likelihood of each of the following outcomes of the requested search. There are many possible outcomes; please rate each outcome independently. (0 = not at all likely; 100 = completely likely)”

The search reveals evidence that the suspect illegally obtained an abortion to end her own pregnancy (e.g., records of obtaining abortion medication outside formal medical care, or related online activity). (0–100%)
The search reveals evidence that the suspect improperly disposed of the fetal remains or concealed the loss following a miscarriage or stillbirth (e.g., records of disposal arrangements made after the loss, or other indications of improper handling of the remains). (0–100%)
The search reveals evidence that the suspect committed an unrelated crime (e.g., stolen credit cards and associated records, or other evidence of a financial crime). (0–100%)
The search reveals nothing illegal or incriminating. (0–100%)

text:
K. Search-Target Endorsement
Instructions: Imagine the same investigation you just read about. Now suppose that, instead of seeking to search the suspect’s phone, the detective stated that there was probable cause to carry out each of the searches described below. For each one, please answer the two questions that follow.

Reverse keyword warrant: A court order directing a technology company to identify any person who recently searched for specified pregnancy-related or abortion-related terms on the company’s search engine.”
Provider text-message content warrant: A warrant served on the suspect’s cellular-service provider compelling disclosure of the content of the suspect’s text messages.
Physical home search: A warrant authorizing law enforcement officers to physically search the suspect’s home.

Participants answered two questions for each target:

Search endorsement: “Would you approve of a law enforcement officer conducting this search?” (Yes / No)
Certainty threshold: “What percentage certain would you have to be that the suspect committed the offense described in the affidavit before approving this search?” (Certainty required, 0–100%)

After all three targets, participants answered one further question for each target:
Instructions: “We have a few more questions about the searches you just considered. For each of the following searches, please rate how likely it is that the search would uncover evidence of the offense, assuming, hypothetically, that the suspect had committed it.”

“If the suspect had indeed committed the offense described in the affidavit, what is the probability that a reverse keyword warrant on online search history would uncover evidence of it?” (0% = not at all likely; 100% = completely likely)
“If the suspect had indeed committed the offense described in the affidavit, what is the probability that a warrant for the suspect’s text-message communications would uncover evidence of it?” (0% = not at all likely; 100% = completely likely)
“If the suspect had indeed committed the offense described in the affidavit, what is the probability that a physical search of the suspect’s residence would uncover evidence of it?” (0% = not at all likely; 100% = completely likely)

title: S1. Deviations from the registration
text:
2. Substitute Mediator (H3c–H3e)
A survey glitch prevented administration of the registered probability-of-guilt item, so the registered H3c–H3e test could not run. After data collection, before analyzing any Study 1 outcome or inspecting likelihood or blame values, I substituted pregnancy-evidence likelihood: the registered 0–100 abortion/disposal likelihood composite also used in E9a–E9b, with the original model, intervals, and support rules. It concerns finding evidence rather than guilt, so I report it as a substitute; foreseeability, which concerns predictability from the detective’s perspective, carries no directional E9 prediction. The timing limits my discretion over the substitute but cannot establish severity for a registered test that could not run. S7 reports the substitute analysis; Chapter 5 reports H3a–H3b and footnotes the unavailable registered H3c–H3e tests.

title: S1. Deviations from the registration
text:
4. Relative Relevance (H1; H4b–H4d)
In place of the registered ten-item mean, the Chapter 5 mediator for H1 and H4b–H4d is relative relevance: the mean of E4a’s items consistent with self-managed abortion (1, 6, and 7) minus the mean of the other items. I changed only the relevance measure; the other specifications and decision rules follow the registration. Because the key fits the self-managed abortion outcome only, relative relevance does not test sense-making after financial-crime evidence (H1b and H4c). I chose the replacement only after seeing the registered results, which reduced the severity of these tests, although the score measures the predicted contrast more directly; their H1a–H1d and H4b–H4d decisions may differ from the registered decisions. The registered results based on the ten-item mean are reported in this supplement.

title: S4. Full results of the manuscript’s models
text:
Notes shared by tables of this section.

Tables 1-S4.1 and 1-S4.11: Scaled (Satorra–Bentler) chi-square with its p; robust CFI; robust RMSEA with its 90% interval; SRMR, as registered for the over-identified model.
Tables 1-S4.1, 1-S4.11 and 1-S4.23: Global fit is reported and changes no model.
Tables 1-S4.1, 1-S4.2, 1-S4.11 and 1-S4.23: RMSEA and its 90% interval: lavaan’s robust RMSEA and its robust interval as lavaan reports them (fitMeasures() rmsea.robust, rmsea.ci.lower.robust and rmsea.ci.upper.robust, at lavaan’s default 90% level).
Tables 1-S4.3 and 1-S4.12: The coefficients retain the variables’ original units. I report robust (Huber–White) standard errors, two-sided normal Wald 95% intervals, and two-sided p values.
Tables 1-S4.3, 1-S4.12 and 1-S4.24: Paths marked equal across contexts are one shared parameter.
Tables 1-S4.3, 1-S4.5, 1-S4.24 and 1-S4.25: Expected evidence = evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion; unexpected evidence = financial-crime evidence; each is contrasted with no information.
Tables 1-S4.3 to 1-S4.6, 1-S4.9, 1-S4.10, 1-S4.12, 1-S4.13, 1-S4.15, 1-S4.18, 1-S4.19, 1-S4.22, 1-S4.24 and 1-S4.25: n per condition, primary sample: Illegal abortion: No information 68, Expected evidence 63, Unexpected evidence 63; Improper disposal: No information 71, Expected evidence 66, Unexpected evidence 67 (all 398 in the analysis).
Tables 1-S4.3, 1-S4.12 and 1-S4.24: β = the standardized estimate (std.all) of the same path; inference and decisions use the unstandardized estimates.
Tables 1-S4.5 and 1-S4.25: The pooled estimates: every path constrained to be equal across the two legal contexts (the registered secondary analysis when both contexts pass the legal-context rule).
Tables 1-S4.6 and 1-S4.15: Each entry is the condition mean with its two-sided 95% Student t interval, from the saved model’s coefficients and covariance on its residual degrees of freedom: with the attitudes, the mean at the attitude means of the participants in the model; without them, the condition mean.
Tables 1-S4.6 and 1-S4.8 to 1-S4.10: Likelihood ratings are in points on the 0–100 scale; foreseeability is in points on the 1–5 scale.
Tables 1-S4.6, 1-S4.9, 1-S4.10, 1-S4.12, 1-S4.13, 1-S4.15, 1-S4.18, 1-S4.19 and 1-S4.22: Expected evidence = evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion; unexpected evidence = financial-crime evidence.
Tables 1-S4.7, 1-S4.16 and 1-S4.20: Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) with the four attitudes as covariates.
Tables 1-S4.7, 1-S4.16 and 1-S4.20: Partial η² = partial eta-squared (η²ₚ) with its 90% CI (noncentral F).
Tables 1-S4.7, 1-S4.16 and 1-S4.20: Adjusted means estimated at covariate mean(s) via emmeans.
Tables 1-S4.7 and 1-S4.16: The bands with the attitudes are the analyses of covariance.
Tables 1-S4.7 and 1-S4.16: The bands without attitudes are the analyses of variance without covariates.
Tables 1-S4.7 and 1-S4.20: The registered tests are the comparisons, not these F tests.
Tables 1-S4.8 and 1-S4.17: Unstandardized slopes of the four attitudes, common to the six conditions, from the saved models with attitudes: judgment points per attitude scale point, with Student t tests and two-sided 95% Student t intervals on the residual degrees of freedom.
Tables 1-S4.9 and 1-S4.10: Differences of adjusted condition means with their standard errors, Student t tests and two-sided 95% Student t intervals on the residual degrees of freedom of each model; no adjustment for multiple comparisons.
Tables 1-S4.9 and 1-S4.18: The models carry the six conditions and no covariate.
Tables 1-S4.9 and 1-S4.18: Reported beside the registered models; decisions are read from the models with attitudes only.
Tables 1-S4.15, 1-S4.17 and 1-S4.18: Decision quality is in points on the 1–7 scale; detective blame, deserved consequences and wrongness are in points on their 0–10 scales.
Tables 1-S4.19 and 1-S4.22: Blame, punishment, the four mental states, responsibility and wrongness are rated on the 1–7 scale; differences are in scale points.

title: S7. RQ3: Exploratory Suspect Judgments
text:
Notes shared by tables of this section.

Tables 1-S7.1 to 1-S7.3: The judgments tested here are rated on the 1–7 scale; differences and means are in scale points.
Tables 1-S7.1 to 1-S7.17: Expected evidence = evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion; unexpected evidence = financial-crime evidence.
Tables 1-S7.1 to 1-S7.3 and 1-S7.5 to 1-S7.18: n per condition, primary sample: Illegal abortion: No information 68, Expected evidence 63, Unexpected evidence 63; Improper disposal: No information 71, Expected evidence 66, Unexpected evidence 67 (all 398 in the analysis).
Tables 1-S7.2 and 1-S7.4: n per condition, sensitivity sample: Illegal abortion: No information 55, Expected evidence 56, Unexpected evidence 54; Improper disposal: No information 56, Expected evidence 62, Unexpected evidence 58 (all 341 in the analysis).
Tables 1-S7.4 and 1-S7.7 to 1-S7.14: Blame, punishment, the four mental states, responsibility and wrongness are rated on the 1–7 scale; differences are in scale points.
Tables 1-S7.5, 1-S7.7, 1-S7.8, 1-S7.14 and 1-S7.15: Intervals: two-sided 95% percentile bootstrap intervals (type 6) from participant resamples stratified within the six conditions, 10,000 attempted and 10,000 usable.
Tables 1-S7.5 and 1-S7.15: The model is just-identified, so it has no global fit.
Tables 1-S7.5, 1-S7.7, 1-S7.14 and 1-S7.15: A letter is supported when its interval lies on the predicted side of zero.
Tables 1-S7.5 and 1-S7.6: Every row of this analysis uses pregnancy-evidence likelihood as the substitute mediator (deviation 2 in S1).
Tables 1-S7.6 and 1-S7.17: Unstandardized estimates in the original units with robust (Huber–White) standard errors, normal Wald 95% intervals and two-sided p.
Tables 1-S7.6 and 1-S7.17: β = the standardized estimate (std.all) of the same path; inference and decisions use the unstandardized estimates.
Tables 1-S7.7 and 1-S7.8: Differences of adjusted outcome-condition means, each the equal-weight average of the two within-context differences, from analyses of covariance with the four attitudes as covariates.
Tables 1-S7.7, 1-S7.8 and 1-S7.14: No item was missing, so no values were imputed.
Tables 1-S7.9, 1-S7.11 and 1-S7.12: Interval: Normal Wald, two-sided 95%; the test statistic and p from the same standard error. n = 398.
Tables 1-S7.9, 1-S7.11 and 1-S7.12: I calculated the comparisons jointly from the model of all four ratings.
Tables 1-S7.9, 1-S7.11 and 1-S7.12: The model has an outcome-condition intercept in each legal context and unrestricted residual covariances.
Tables 1-S7.9, 1-S7.11 and 1-S7.12: The comparisons hold attitudes at their means and include variation in that attitude reference in their standard errors.

Tables 1-S9.1 and 1-S9.4: Expected evidence = evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion; unexpected evidence = financial-crime evidence.
Tables 1-S9.1 and 1-S9.4: n per condition, primary sample: Illegal abortion: No information 68, Expected evidence 63, Unexpected evidence 63; Improper disposal: No information 71, Expected evidence 66, Unexpected evidence 67 (all 398 in the analysis).



Figure 1-S9.1
Adjusted mean certainty required for each search target, overall and by outcome information


Note. Adjusted mean certainty required for each search target from the joint model of the three certainty ratings, with attitudes at their primary-sample means. The left panel compares the targets overall, with adjacent differences corresponding to H5a and H5b. In the right panel, the two legal contexts have equal weight within each outcome condition. Error bars represent two-sided 95% t confidence intervals for the means, based on the model’s residual degrees of freedom. The interval calculation combines the joint model covariance and the sampling covariance of the attitude means, as in the registered comparisons. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.

title: Study 2
text:
About this document
This part includes the supplementary tables and figures for Study 2. For the main findings, see Chapter 5. The supplementary materials cover data cleaning and missing data, descriptive and preliminary analyses, manipulation checks, RQ1 through RQ5, and the sensitivity sample. Within S1 through S9, I grouped each analysis with its hypotheses and comparisons. The tables and figures reproduce the final Study 2 estimates.
Table and figure numbers identify the study and the section. For example, Table 2-S4.1 begins S4. The H4a–H4h comparisons and adjusted H4 means are in S6.

title: Study 2 Design and Materials
text:
Condition Materials
In Study 2, I adapted the civil-juror case materials of Casper et al. (1989) and Robbennolt & Sobus (1997) to a pregnancy-loss arrest. Participants acted as jurors in a fictional § 1983 false-arrest suit and read one randomly assigned case file. Table S2D.1 links the design to the study materials, and Figure S2D.1 shows the six conditions.
The Materials and Measures chapter reproduces the stimulus variations, survey questions, and response scales. The materials hub provides document-image previews. The preregistration and registered materials PDF provide the planned design and wording; the deviations record documents departures.

title: Study 2 Materials and Measures
text:
F. Evidence Interpretation
Participants rate each of the ten facts on two dimensions: relevance and incrimination. Both use a 9-point scale. Relevance ratings precede incrimination ratings, and item order is randomized within each dimension. Participants complete these ratings once, after receiving the assigned outcome information.

Items shown to Ps in the Stereotypical variant (SMA-prototype):

That an anonymous coworker reported Ms. Johnston had said she used pills ordered online to handle it at home.
That Ms. Johnston experienced cramping and heavy bleeding at home.
That Ms. Johnston said the pregnancy passed in the bathroom, that she panicked and flushed the toilet, disposing of the remains through the residential plumbing.
That fetal remains were recovered from the residential plumbing, consistent with a fetus of approximately 20 weeks.
That Ms. Johnston did not call 911 or seek in-person medical care.
That Ms. Johnston was 18 years old, unmarried, and had no children.
That Ms. Johnston lived with a roommate, who was out of town on the day of the event.
That Ms. Johnston did not tell anyone on the day of the event.
That Ms. Johnston kept a hair appointment that afternoon and worked her shifts over the next two days.
That Detective Snyder had 14 years of experience with the Millfield Police Department.

That an anonymous coworker reported Ms. Johnston had said she handled it at home by herself.

That Ms. Johnston was 31 years old, married, and had two school-age children.

That Detective Snyder had 14 years of experience with the Millfield Police Department.

title: Study 2 Materials and Measures
text:
K. Damages (Robbennolt & Sobus, 1997)
Preamble. As the juror in this case, you are now asked to decide what amount of money damages, if any, Ms. Johnston (the plaintiff) should receive from Detective Snyder. There are two kinds of damages, and you will be asked about each separately. If you believe Ms. Johnston should receive no damages, you may enter $0. In closing argument, Ms. Johnston’s counsel asked the jury to award $75,000 in compensatory damages and $500,000 in punitive damages. You are not required to award these amounts; the amount you award, if any, is entirely for you to decide. Compensatory damages. If you decide Ms. Johnston (the plaintiff) should recover, compensatory damages are the amount of money that will fairly compensate her for the harm you find she sustained as a direct result of the arrest. This may include out-of-pocket losses, loss of liberty, emotional distress, personal humiliation, and damage to her reputation. You must not award compensatory damages as a way of punishing Detective Snyder or out of sympathy. How much, if anything, do you award Ms. Johnston in compensatory damages? Response: numeric text entry (whole dollars). No default. Punitive damages. Punitive damages are separate from compensatory damages and are not meant to compensate Ms. Johnston (the plaintiff) further. If you find that Detective Snyder’s conduct was malicious or showed reckless indifference to Ms. Johnston’s rights, you may — but are not required to — award punitive damages, to punish him and to discourage him and other officers from similar conduct in the future. Any amount you award should bear a reasonable relationship to the harm caused. How much, if anything, do you award Ms. Johnston in punitive damages? Response: numeric text entry (whole dollars). No default.
Severity of consequences.
“How serious are the consequences of what happened in this case?” (1 = not at all serious; 7 = extremely serious)

text:
L. Manipulation Checks

Stereotypicality Manipulation Check
“According to the case file you read, the fact pattern Detective Snyder was investigating most closely matched:”
Response options:

An 18-year-old unmarried woman with no children, who lived with a roommate who was out of town on the day of the event, who did not tell anyone that day, and whose coworker reported she had said she used pills ordered online to handle it at home. (correct for Stereotypical)
A 31-year-old married woman with two school-age children, who lived with her husband and children, who told her husband on the day of the event, and whose coworker reported she had said she handled it at home by herself. (correct for Non-stereotypical)
A criminal disposal of remains following an unrelated event.
None of the above; the fact pattern did not point clearly to any of these.
I’m not sure.




Outcome Manipulation Check
“Did the case file include a summary of what was discovered after the arrest about the cause of the pregnancy loss, and if so, what did it say?”
Response options:

Yes: the summary said a post-arrest joint investigation by the Carter County coroner’s and prosecutor’s offices, including review of records subpoenaed from an online telehealth service, determined that the pregnancy loss had been induced by mifepristone and misoprostol pills Ms. Johnston had obtained through that service. (correct for SMA-outcome)
Yes: the summary said a post-arrest joint investigation by the Carter County coroner’s and prosecutor’s offices, including review of medical records from Ms. Johnston’s obstetric provider, determined that the pregnancy loss had been a spontaneous miscarriage of a clinically wanted pregnancy with no evidence of any self-induced cause. (correct for NCM-outcome)
Yes: the summary said no additional forensic, medical, or investigative records bearing on the cause of the loss have been generated since the arrest, and the cause has not been formally determined. (correct for None-outcome)
I don’t remember.




Content-Recognition Check
“Which of the following facts was NOT in the case scenario you read about?”
Response options:


The Millfield Police Department received an anonymous tip about Ms. Johnston.


Detective Snyder conducted a knock-and-talk interview with Ms. Johnston at her residence.


Ms. Johnston’s mother contacted the police about her behavior. (correct answer — this fact was NOT in the case)


Detective Snyder interviewed Ms. Johnston’s coworker Andi Donen at the retail store.





Resultant-Surprise Check (Exploratory)

Resultant surprise. “How surprising was the post-arrest agreed-facts summary, given the arrest report and Detective Snyder’s testimony?” (1 = not at all surprising; 7 = extremely surprising)
Expectation fit (reverse-scored). “How well did the agreed-facts summary fit what you would have expected based on the arrest report and testimony?” (1 = did not fit at all; 7 = fit extremely well)

        Note. b = unstandardized estimate, primary sample; Adjusted = with the four attitudes (and error preference in the consequence equation); Unadjusted = without them. Coefficients: the labeled parameters of the registered three-equation model, with robust (Huber-White) Wald 95% intervals; the foreseeability-to-blame coefficient is equal across the two evidence conditions within each outcome, and the blame-to-consequence coefficient is common to the six conditions, as registered. Products: the foreseeability-to-blame coefficient under each outcome times the common blame-to-consequence coefficient. Remaining direct difference: the analysis's average, over the included SMA and NCM participants in their own evidence condition, of the consequence equation's condition-specific terms under SMA minus under NCM (the common blame and error-preference terms cancel). Both take percentile bootstrap 95% intervals. Percentile bootstrap: 10000 within-condition participant resamples; usable attempts per quantity: 10000 (failed attempts are not replaced). lavaan estimator MLR (estimator ML with robust.huber.white standard errors, missing = ml). Scaled fit of the adjusted model: scaled χ²(25) = 24.31, p = .501, CFI = 1.000, TLI = 1.007, RMSEA = 0.000 (90% CI [0.000, 0.106]), SRMR = 0.038. No model variable was missing, so no auxiliary items were used. Letter = the registered read; the no-information coefficient and the three products carry no registered direction and are reported without a support gate.

        Note. I examined whether the SMA − NCM award difference varied with abortion attitudes using a logistic model for any award and a Gamma model with a log link for positive amounts. In this primary adjusted two-part model, each part has six condition intercepts and six abortion-attitude slopes. Within each part, the plaintiff-blame, officer-blame, and other three attitude slopes are common across the six conditions. The Gamma model has one dispersion parameter. For each attitude probe, I calculated the SMA − NCM differences in award probability, positive award amount, and expected award. Expected award is the product of probability and positive amount, including zero awards. Predictions cover the included SMA and NCM participants (n = 213), each in their own evidence condition with equal weight, with attitudes set to the probe. Probe values are the participants’ abortion-attitude mean (3.31) minus and plus one sample SD (1.77). Both lie inside the observed range common to all four SMA and NCM conditions, 1.00 to 6.86. As specified in the registered analysis supplement, the last row subtracts the lower-score difference from the higher-score difference. The 95% interval covers only the expected-award difference. Each participant percentile bootstrap attempt refits both model parts and recalculates its attitude mean and SD. Of 10000 participant resamples drawn within conditions, 9959 were usable per quantity; failed attempts were not replaced. Award-probability and positive-award differences are descriptive components of the same predictions, without intervals. E5b has no registered direction or support gate. Decision for E5b: estimates reported; no registered decision rule.

title: Deviations Records
text:
About this document
This part includes the deviations record of each study: Pilot Study 1, Pilot Study 2, Study 1 and Study 2. The deviations records are included in this supplement (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23424192). The registrations are on the Open Science Framework.

title: Pilot Study 1 Deviations Record
text:
2. Random-effects structure for the RH7 models
These entries compare the completed Pilot Study 01 analyses with the registration form, task description, and study measures posted on the project’s Open Science Framework page. The Pilot 01 manuscript reports the analyses as conducted; this record supplies the separate account of departures in the supplement (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23424192).
Each participant judged the same 20 card-sorting scenarios. After finalizing the scenarios, and before the confirmatory analysis, I added a scenario random intercept to both RH7 logistic models. Both models also included a participant random intercept. Neither registration entry called for a scenario intercept: RH7.1 named a participant intercept, and RH7.2 gave no random-effects formula. For RH5.1, by contrast, I entered each feature separately as a fixed predictor, with only a participant random intercept.

title: Pilot Study 1 Deviations Record
section: 3. Direction of the Modified Abortion Attitudes Scale
text:
3. Direction of the Modified Abortion Attitudes Scale
Higher sums on the Modified Abortion Attitudes Scale (Sloan, 1983) indicate stronger pro-abortion attitudes after reverse-keying items 1, 3, 4, 7, 9, 12, and 14. The RH4.1 and RH4.2 labels reverse this scoring direction: a score one standard deviation above the mean is described as “more restrictive.” It is more permissive; one standard deviation below the mean is more restrictive. Cleaning and analyses used this scoring direction: negative RH4.1/RH4.2 coefficients and an RH7.1 odds ratio below 1 represented the predicted harsher or more criminalizing judgments with more restrictive attitudes. RH7.2 predicted a stronger association for normative than descriptive judgments. Correcting the labels changed neither the measure nor these four tests.

title: Pilot Study 1 Deviations Record
section: 4. Overlap between the two narrative coders
text:
4. Overlap between the two narrative coders
Coder 1 rated 188 and coder 2 rated 199 narratives, covering all 324 with 63 overlapping. Reliability for the 14 holistic Phase 3 variables used this overlap after excluding unusable narratives and missing codes.
Instead of two ratings per narrative as the coding plan required, I assigned packets of 198 and 199 to reduce the workload. Both included 73 shared narratives: 10 practice and 63 training (about 20% of 314 non-practice narratives). Seeded allocation split the remaining 251 narratives into sets of 125 and 126. I retained agreed or single-coder codes and set disagreements to missing. After exclusions, 279 narratives had usable mental-state codes for RH2.2 and RH3.1.
Coder time constraints prevented the registered retraining and another pilot coding pass. I reported reliability in full and treated results relying on low-reliability codes as exploratory. Codebook refinement was carried forward to subsequent studies.

title: Pilot Study 1 Deviations Record
section: 5. Specification of the RH5.1 scenario-feature model
text:
5. Specification of the RH5.1 scenario-feature model
Following the working plan, I fitted mental state, medical intervention, pregnancy outcome, care-seeking, and abortion-pill use separately: is_crime ~ feature + (1 | participant_id). RH5.1 named six features without specifying joint or separate entry. In the five-feature joint specification, sought care coincided with medical intervention and delayed care with negligence. Both care-seeking coefficients were absent from the output; it did not establish that all requested effects were estimated or diagnostic criteria were met.
For the single-feature fits, I replaced the 13-level method variable, which had several levels containing one scenario and complete separation, with an abortion-pill indicator for scenarios 1, 2, 4, and 10. I excluded gestational age because 16 of the 20 scenarios did not specify it. The post hoc models predicted judgments from new participants on the same scenarios; they did not separate independent or causal cue effects. I continued to select main-study scenarios for broad disagreement.

title: Pilot Study 1 Deviations Record
section: 6. Change of reference source for the real-world-case half of Exploratory 3
text:
6. Change of reference source for the real-world-case half of Exploratory 3
Herold and Sisson (2019) supplied a comparison for depicted methods, but no distribution of plotlines referring to actual cases. I mapped the 36 visually depicted procedures (24 surgical, 7 medication, and 5 other) onto the four Section F (methodtype) categories. For the Section J (realcase) comparison, I used Pregnancy Justice (2023, The Rise of Pregnancy Criminalization), which documented 1,396 U.S. pregnancy-criminalization cases in 2006–2022, with charge information for 97.8%. Among cases with known charges, approximately 84% involved criminal child neglect, abuse, or endangerment; 6% feticide, murder, or manslaughter; 2% tampering with remains or abuse of a corpse; and 1% legally unauthorized abortion. More than 90% of all census cases involved substance-use allegations. Because the prompts balanced crime categories, narrative shares could not estimate participants’ beliefs about crime frequencies. I used Pregnancy Justice (2026, After Pregnancy Loss) for loss-related examples and framing in this descriptive comparison. The reference change left realcase and RH1–RH7 unchanged.

title: Pilot Study 1 Deviations Record
section: 7. Scope of the RH1 chi-square variable family
text:
7. Scope of the RH1 chi-square variable family
I applied the registered Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment to 67 tests of automated variables (43 Phase 1 and 24 Phase 2) instead of the planned 81. Associations involving the 14 holistic Phase 3 codes were exploratory: only one code provided interpretable evidence of adequate reliability, and I had not completed the required refinement and recoding. The parallel verdict-condition tests were descriptive and used the same 67 variables.

title: Pilot Study 1 Deviations Record
section: 8. Feature screening in the RH1 prototype analysis
text:
8. Feature screening in the RH1 prototype analysis
For clustering only, I added an unregistered screen to the 67 automated codes. I removed defagecat (identical to defagespec under presence coding) and nchars (nearly identical to namedchars). Adapting Wiener et al.’s (2002, pp. 129–130) story-index screen, I retained features present in more than one-third and no more than two-thirds of each crime category’s narratives. This left 9 features for self-managed abortion, 7 for fetal homicide, and 9 each for chemical endangerment and improper disposal.

title: Pilot Study 1 Deviations Record
section: 9. Selection of the number of clusters in the RH1 prototype analysis
text:
9. Selection of the number of clusters in the RH1 prototype analysis
The archived OSF response required at least two crime categories to satisfy “silhouette width > 0.25 or gap-statistic support for k > 2”. The response did not specify how to choose k; I selected the two-, three-, or four-cluster solution with the largest average silhouette width in each crime category. Silhouette is undefined for one cluster (Tibshirani et al., 2001, p. 418). Silhouette and the gap statistic selected two clusters in each category; silhouette widths were .285 for self-managed abortion, .384 for fetal homicide, .256 for chemical endangerment, and .241 for improper disposal.
Only improper disposal failed the archived rule: its silhouette was below the cutoff and its gap result did not satisfy k > 2. The local registration, working plan, and analysis used k ≥ 2, counting all four categories rather than three; both readings met the minimum of two.

title: Pilot Study 1 Deviations Record
section: 11. Reliability statistics for ordered holistic codes
text:
11. Reliability statistics for ordered holistic codes
Five nominally categorical codes had ordered values: Model Penal Code mental state, socioeconomic status, pregnancy wantedness, partner role, and healthcare-provider role. The registration says “the target thresholds are Cohen’s kappa for categorical codes and intraclass correlation for dimensional ratings” and “If thresholds are not met, the codebook will be refined and coders will be retrained.” I reported ICCs as well as kappa for these five codes and removed the not-specified category, whose agreement had counted absence of a construct toward reliability.
None provided interpretable evidence of meeting its target. Both coders specified socioeconomic status in only six narratives, partner role in nine, and healthcare-provider role in ten. Their coefficients are included for completeness; such sparse bases establish neither reliability nor unreliability.

title: Pilot Study 1 Deviations Record
text:
15. Reinstated submission
I preregistered a stopping rule of 80 completions. One submission that Prolific’s bot and LLM authenticity check had initially flagged was found to have been flagged in error and was reinstated, so the analytic sample was 81 rather than the registered 80. The five other Prolific exclusions remained, and the registered attention-check criterion excluded no participant.

title: Pilot Study 2 Deviations Record
text:
1. Power-script coding
I corrected pilot02_power_scripts.R to effects-code outcome and dummy-code timing and vignette, with non-criminal miscarriage as the reference vignette. I reported the existing power estimates without rerunning the simulations.

title: Pilot Study 2 Deviations Record
text:
4. Analysis models

4.2 Search-target random effects
Because each participant rated the three targets only once, during the first vignette, I omitted the registered target slopes but retained the participant random intercept for RH7.1, RH7.2, E7.5, and E7.7.


4.3 Complete-case covariate models
For E4.1–E4.3, I required scores on all six covariates: abortion attitudes, punishment attitudes, hostile sexism, benevolent sexism, religiosity, and political ideology. Multi-item scores required at least 80% item completion.
The registration instead states: “For variables with fewer than 5% missing values, we will impute the missing values using multiple imputation by chained equations (Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011) and analyze the completed data. If a variable has more than 5% missing values, we will report the extent of missing data and analyze only cases with complete data on that variable.” I used complete cases even below 5% missingness, as specified before collection.


4.4 Exploratory intervals
I reported posterior 95% HDIs for officer-model serial mediation, four-mediator parallel mediation of blame, and parallel trait mediation of endorsed punishment, as specified for these Bayesian multilevel models. Only the four-stage chain matched the preamble’s bootstrap description; I used a bias-corrected interval on the product of participant-level regression coefficients (5,000 resamples).


4.6 Priors
I used proper normal(0, s) coefficient priors in each response’s units and LKJ(2) random-effect correlation priors. The brms power calls used flat coefficient priors, as the supplement described, so their power figures were approximate for these fits. I did not establish whether they were conservative. I retained default weakly informative priors for the blavaan factor model.


4.7 Reading the convergence gate
Simulation fits continued to sample one participant intercept–post-search-slope correlation inefficiently after twelvefold chain extensions. I therefore applied the convergence criteria to the registered estimands within each imputation: R-hat < 1.01, effective sample sizes > 400, and zero divergences (Vehtari et al., 2021). RH1.2 was supported only under this narrower reading of the registered “all parameters” requirement.


4.8 Joint likelihood and decision-quality responses
I combined likelihood (RH1.1/RH2.1) and decision quality (RH4.1/RH4.2) in one pre-post model, following my reading of the filed answers rather than the unposted registry’s separate models. I estimated a residual correlation with its default prior, keeping E4.1’s directed analysis separate. Requiring complete data on both responses could change the sample and estimates; registered contrasts and support rules were unchanged.

title: Pilot Study 2 Deviations Record
text:
6. Authenticity screening and admission
Participant submissions on Prolific were not screened until after payment; as a result, some paid submissions were later excluded from analysis.

title: Pilot Study 2 Deviations Record
section: 7. Convergence remedies before the likelihood correction
text:
7. Convergence remedies before the likelihood correction
Because some initial models failed the convergence criteria, I reran serial models with more iterations and withheld support for hypotheses based on other unrefitted models.

7.8 Participant-Mean Likelihood Equations and Model Convergence
I included each participant’s mean likelihood rating once in its mediator equation, as specified in the registered model. For H5a, the first mediator equation included 309 participant means, and the negligence and blame equations each included 927 scenario ratings.
I fit the models with four chains per data set, using five imputed data sets except for the analysis without exclusions, which used complete cases. I increased the number of iterations as needed for convergence without changing the priors. All nine models met the registered convergence criteria: R̂ < 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes > 400, and no divergent transitions.

title: Pilot Study 2 Deviations Record
section: 9.1 RH1.4: comparing the same relevance items
text:
9.1 RH1.4: comparing the same relevance items
The registered consistency coefficient mixed item and outcome differences. HACE included consistent and inconsistent items; all HUCE items were inconsistent. In the criminal-miscarriage and self-managed-abortion vignettes, the HACE-inconsistent set contained only background items 3 and 10. A larger decline under HUCE could therefore contribute to the intended relative-relevance effect.
After seeing this pattern, I applied the HACE key to both outcomes and fitted:
relevance_item ~ timing * outcome * key_consistent + vignette + timing:vignette + (1 + timing | participant_id) + (1 | vignette:item)
The three-way interaction compares HACE − HUCE change for key-consistent versus key-inconsistent items. Across equally weighted vignettes, the estimated pre-to-post change for key-consistent items was −0.01 (95% HDI [−0.19, 0.17]) after HACE and −1.20 [−1.38, −1.02] after HUCE. For key-inconsistent items, relevance changed by −0.11 [−0.31, 0.10] after HACE and −0.52 [−0.72, −0.32] after HUCE. Thus, the HUCE decline was larger for items that would have fitted the pregnancy outcome.
I reported RH1.4 as supported using the same-item model (three-way interaction = 0.77, 95% HDI [0.52, 1.02]). The original timing × item-consistency estimate also met the registered rule (0.47, 95% HDI [0.31, 0.64]). I chose the revised model after inspecting the raw means, reducing test severity (Lakens, 2024).
