title: Study 1 Deviations Record
text:
Evaluation of the Study 1 and Study 2 departures
The comparison is with Open Science Framework registration 93w7p, its form, materials, exploratory supplement, and power-analysis script.
I use Lakens (2024) to distinguish severity from validity. Each entry identifies what I could choose and what I had seen when choosing it. Those conditions bear on severity—the ability to support a true hypothesis and withhold support from a false one—separately from validity. Improving validity can leave severity higher, lower, or unchanged. Reasons may overlap: unforeseen events, mistakes in the preregistration or study, missing information, violated untested assumptions, and falsified auxiliary hypotheses. I assess severity for every entry and validity for mistakes and the last two categories. Selecting a rule because it excludes zero introduces selection bias under either inferential framework.

title: Study 1 Deviations Record
section: 2. Missing guilt measure and the H3c–H3e substitute
text:
2. Missing guilt measure and the H3c–H3e substitute
H3c–H3e predict a route from outcome information to blame “through how likely participants think it is that the suspect committed the offense”: positive after SMA evidence and negative after financial-crime evidence versus no outcome information, and more positive after SMA than financial-crime evidence. The intended mediator was “Based on the evidence available at the time the warrant was sought, what is the probability that the suspect committed the crime the detective suspects her of committing?” on a 0–100 scale (supplement, “Probability and blame (H3c–H3e)”, Figure 4).
A survey error kept participants from seeing the guilt item, so I could not run the registered H3c–H3e test or assess its severity. After data collection ended, and before I had analyzed any Study 1 outcome or looked at any likelihood or blame rating, I chose pregnancy-evidence likelihood as the substitute. This registered 0–100 composite combined the abortion and disposal likelihood ratings and was also a mediator in E9a–E9b. It concerned the likelihood that the search would find pregnancy-related evidence, not the suspect’s guilt. I did not use the foreseeability index, which concerned how predictable the search outcome was from the detective’s perspective; the registration made no directional prediction through it (E9).
I fitted the registered mediation model in two legal-context groups, with four attitude covariates in both equations, and repeated it without attitudes. Support depended on indirect effects alone. The indirect effects and their difference received percentile 95% intervals from 10,000 usable participant bootstrap samples; individual paths had robust Wald intervals.

title: Study 1 Deviations Record
section: 4. Relative relevance for H1 and H4b–H4d
text:
4. Relative relevance for H1 and H4b–H4d
I used E4a’s existing key to replace the ten-item mean with mean relevance of items consistent with self-managed abortion (SMA; items 1, 6, and 7) minus that of the remaining items. Pooling all ten items could conceal a shift toward outcome-fitting evidence. E4a examined that contrast at item level, without likelihood judgments. Using the SMA key left financial-crime sense-making untested (H1b and H4c). I changed only the relevance measure; other specifications and support criteria followed the registration. I read support from the primary sample and reported registered ten-item-mean results alongside each affected hypothesis.
I recognized this preregistration mistake after seeing the registered results, although it was knowable before collection. Choosing the relative score then reduced test severity and could change H1a–H1d and H4b–H4d decisions; the score more directly represented the predicted contrast.

Purpose
I compared the analyses with registration b53yg, its form, study materials, exploratory supplement, and two power-analysis scripts.

title: Study 2 Deviations Record
section: 1. Comparisons added after registration and the procedure that tests them
text:
1. Comparisons added after registration and the procedure that tests them
What was posted: a directional hypothesis receives support if its 95% confidence interval excludes zero in the predicted direction, “with no correction for multiple comparisons” (supplement, “Preamble”). Confidence in the probable-cause ruling is among the judgments that “will be summarized descriptively and are not analyzed inferentially in Study 2” (supplement, “Additional within-model and descriptive reports”).
After seeing the Study 02 results, I added 12 comparisons: all three pairwise differences among SMA, NCM, and no outcome information in a signed probable cause–confidence score, from a model with the H5d ANCOVA specification.
I signed the confidence rating by the ruling: positive for finding probable cause and negative for rejecting it. Thus equally confident opposite rulings receive opposite signs on the −100 to 100 score, rather than sharing a high 0–100 confidence value. Three outcome pairs, two covariate specifications (with or without the four attitudes), and two samples (N = 320 and registered sensitivity N = 212) yielded 12 comparisons. I regarded the registration’s omission of these comparisons as an error because relating the probable-cause ruling to confidence was central to the study’s purpose.
For each model, I tested the family of three comparisons—SMA–no information, NCM–no information, and SMA–NCM—with Fisher’s protected least significant difference (LSD) procedure (Levin et al., 1994). I first used the same fitted model and covariance matrix to test whether the SMA–no-information and NCM–no-information differences were jointly zero, with a Wald F(2, residual df) test. I regarded a pairwise difference as significant only if both its own p value and the omnibus p value were below .05. For reporting, I used the larger of these values as the protected p value. I decided on this procedure after seeing the results.
I also checked each model’s family of three comparisons with single-step Tukey-adjusted p values from the same fit and covariance. Of the 12 added comparisons, six were significant under LSD and three had Tukey-adjusted p values below .05. The discordant comparisons were:

Adjusted primary sample, SMA–no information: p = .038 (LSD), .078 (Tukey).
Adjusted primary sample, SMA–NCM: .038, .057.
Unadjusted sensitivity sample, SMA–NCM: p = .024 (LSD), .062 (Tukey).

I reported the added comparisons as post hoc tests with low severity because I chose the procedure after seeing its results. Registered analyses and support decisions were unchanged (supplement, “Exploratory analyses”).

title: Study 2 Deviations Record
section: 2. Relative relevance as the mediator of H2a–H2d
text:
2. Relative relevance as the mediator of H2a–H2d
For H2a–H2d, I replaced pooled relevance with a relative score in the registered observed-score model. Within each record, I subtracted mean relevance of facts fitting natural miscarriage (NCM) from mean relevance of facts fitting self-managed abortion (SMA), excluding facts fitting neither.
I chose this mediator after seeing the Study 02 results and classified the facts after seeing E1b. Both choices reduced test severity. I retained the other model specifications and support criteria, used the adjusted primary analysis for support decisions, and reported the registered latent-factor results alongside it.
